soil-env-181.title: Everything soil does for people and ecosystems
soil-env-181.text: About 50% of people live in houses built from soil. That is one of many jobs a {{ref:soil-found-077}} does, and together they are called soil functions: the general capabilities that matter for agriculture, the environment, nature protection, landscape architecture and urban uses. For food and biomass, soil stores and supplies nutrients, holds water in its pores and moderates temperature. It is a habitat and gene reserve for many organisms, and it turns the remains of dead plants and animals into simpler mineral forms other life can use. Soil also governs whether rain runs off or recharges aquifers, purifies septic drain field wastes and stores atmospheric carbon in organic matter. It supplies raw materials, and it carries cultural meaning, giving a sense of place and preserving artifacts of the past. Productive soil is limited in area, so extracting it needs to be controlled.

soil-phys-032.title: Biological soil crust: a living skin on bare ground
soil-phys-032.text: Across about 12% of the earth's landmass, the ground between plants is covered by a living skin. A biological soil crust is a community of fungi, lichens, cyanobacteria, bryophytes and algae in the open spaces between vascular plants. Only cyanobacteria and cyanolichens fix nitrogen, so what a crust contributes depends on its makeup. Its carbon cycling happens only when it is wet. Crusts darken the surface, which lowers albedo, and their roughness traps dust. The easiest way to keep them is to remove stressors such as grazing, or to protect them from disturbance.

soil-found-051.title: Soil texture: the sand, silt and clay recipe
soil-found-051.text:
Rub a moist pinch of soil between your fingers and you are already measuring its texture. Soil texture is the quality of a soil set by its make-up of sand, silt and clay particles. It considers only particles less than two millimetres across. Texture classes rest on the percentages of the three; the USDA and WRB systems use 12 classes and the UK-ADAS system 11. Albert Atterberg proposed the first classification, the international system, in 1905.

Texture can be judged by feel or measured, for example by the hydrometer method, which rests on Stokes' law. Because it is fixed by the mineral part of a soil, it does not change with farming, unlike soil structure.

Texture matters because it shapes so much else. Field capacity, the soil water content best suited to plant growth, rises as particles get finer, from sand to clay. Texture helps decide which crops suit a soil and predicts its response to drought or its lime needs. Together with structure it is called a master variable, since it directly influences many other properties. A clayey soil has more surface area, cation exchange capacity, total porosity and organic matter than a sandy one, but less macroporosity. The first of these traits comes from {{ref:soil-found-040}}, and the proportions of all the components are laid out in {{ref:soil-found-078}}.

soil-found-027.title: What a soil's color says about its history
soil-found-027.text: A soil keeps its history on its surface, and color is how it shows it. Dark brown or black usually means high organic matter, which coats mineral particles and darkens them; accumulated charcoal also turns soil black. An Illinois handheld chart links nearly black soil to 3.5-7% organic matter, dark brown to 2-3% and yellowish brown to 1.5-2.5%. Red points to iron accumulation or oxidation in well-aerated soil, and yellow also reflects iron, in less oxygen-rich settings. Gray or blue marks saturated, anaerobic soil where iron has been reduced or depleted. Green can come from iron reduction or from minerals such as glauconite, melanterite and celadonite. White is common where salts or carbonates accumulate, often in arid places, and jarosite can color acidic soils yellow. A B horizon takes its color mainly from iron oxides, usually brownish or reddish. Sodium helps humus disperse and reach more minerals, so it influences how deep the dark color extends.

soil-form-172.title: Hydrolysis: how water cracks minerals open
soil-form-172.text:
Water does more than wet a mineral; it can break it. Hydrolysis is any chemical reaction in which a water molecule breaks one or more chemical bonds. One fragment of the split molecule gains a hydrogen ion and the other gains a hydroxide. It is the reverse of condensation, which joins molecules by removing water.

The lab manual says all minerals weather this way, and that hydrolysis is the primary reaction releasing most plant nutrient elements from minerals. In one example, orthoclase and water yield an aluminum silicate, K+ and OH-. This is a main route of {{ref:soil-found-058}}.

Hydrolysis also drives soil chemistry. Metal ions in water form aqua ions that act as acids: trivalent Al3+ and Fe3+ are weak acids with a pKa comparable to acetic acid, while Na+ hydrolyses almost imperceptibly. In acid sulfate soils, loosely bound Al3+ and Fe3+ and sparingly soluble sulfates such as jarosite release H+ this way. In alkali soils the carbonate anion hydrolyses to bicarbonate and hydroxyl ions, raising pH. The enzyme urease catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea, and highly alkaline soils, pH about 8.2 or higher, increase it.

soil-form-141.title: Feldspar: the rock mineral that becomes clay
soil-form-141.text: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust and 41% of the continental crust by weight. They are rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals that also contain cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium. The commonest are the sodium-calcium plagioclase feldspars and the potassium-sodium alkali feldspars. Formed at high temperature, they are unstable at the surface, especially plagioclase, so they weather easily. Hydrolysis, described in {{ref:soil-form-172}}, turns them into clay minerals including illite, smectite and kaolinite, and because feldspars are so abundant, clays are abundant too. Clay-replaced feldspar looks chalky beside glassy unweathered grains. Feldspar-rich sediment therefore points to little chemical weathering before burial.

soil-form-034.title: Cryoturbation: how frost churns the ground
soil-form-034.text:
In the frozen north, the soil mixes itself. Cryoturbation is frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in permafrost soils. It occurs to some degree in most Gelisols, whose name comes from Latin gelare, to freeze.

Autumn freezing forms ice wedges in the most erodible parts of the parent rock. In summer the active layer lets loosened material move both down and up. Moisture moves from the warm surface to the cold permafrost table, drying the upper soil into a granular structure with ice lenses. These lenses grow by drawing unfrozen water along a thermal gradient, displacing and mixing mineral and organic material at the ice-water interface. Separation of coarse from fine material produces patterned ground.

It is the dominant force in the active layer and tends to make it uniform in composition. It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys: Turbels show it in over one-third of the active layer, with distorted horizon boundaries, Orthels in less. In frost boils it can bring base-rich water to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients. In effect, ice scrambles the layers described in {{ref:soil-found-001}}.

soil-form-158.title: How a soil changes as it grows old
soil-form-158.text:
A soil has an age, and it shows. Parent material has no horizons. A young soil, about 10 to 1,000 years old, has a slight profile. A mature soil, 1,000 to 10,000 years, has a well-developed one, and an old soil, 10,000 to 100,000 years, an extensive one. Typical profiles run C R, then A C R, then O A Bt C R, then O A E Bs C R.

The chemistry changes too. In a young soil humus accumulates and carbonates leach. In a mature soil humus peaks and clays leach, with maximum illuviation. In an old soil humus declines, carbonates are gone and the surface is very acidic. Crop productivity follows: low to moderate in young soil, maximal in mature soil and low in old soil.

Once vegetation grew, nitrogen entered from rain and from lichens, algae and legumes, and organic matter built a dark A horizon as rain leached calcium and magnesium carbonates. Where soils stay highly calcareous, the lime limits clay leaching and slows development. On permeable material, clay moved from the A into the B and formed an argillic horizon. This is {{ref:soil-form-047}} at work.

soil-form-155.title: Four ways soils gain, lose, change and move material
soil-form-155.text:
What makes soil different from a layer of sediment? Four groups of processes, through which the {{ref:soil-form-043}} work: additions, losses, transformations and translocations. How far they have gone helps tell soils apart.

Additions include organic matter, fertilizers, dust and other mineral soil arriving. Losses are soil moved away by wind or water, or chemical compounds leached, eroded or harvested. Transformations are the chemical or physical weathering of particles or components. Weathering releases ions from minerals or turns them into secondary minerals, which may reform deeper in the soil; ions lost altogether are leached.

Translocations are movements of organic or mineral components between horizons. Eluviation removes material from a horizon and illuviation deposits it; clay, and iron and aluminium organic complexes, move down with soil water. Mixing, or turbation, is also a transfer, caused by organisms or by physical agents such as clay shrink-swell and freeze-thaw.

soil-form-159.title: Reading runoff from slope and texture
soil-form-159.text: How fast will rain run off a field? Percent slope is rise over run times 100, read directly with an Abney level or clinometer held parallel to the slope. Runoff rises with slope and falls with infiltration rate. Granular, porous soils shed less water than massive, low-porosity ones, because more water infiltrates. A moister soil saturates sooner and so runs off sooner, while plant cover intercepts raindrops and reduces erosion. In the field table, slopes of 0-1% give very slow runoff for all textures, 6-12% gives rapid runoff for loams but very rapid for clays, and over 18% is very rapid for all textures.

soil-form-156.title: From summit to toeslope: positions on a hillside
soil-form-156.text: A hillside is not one soil but a sequence. The summit is the level top of an upland feature, and the shoulder is the convex, erosional edge leading to the backslope. The backslope is the steepest part, shaped mainly by mass wasting and running water. Below it, the footslope is gently inclined and concave, where colluvium and alluvium accumulate, and the toeslope is a constructional surface where alluvium collects. Beyond lies a flood plain, built of sediment deposited during floods, and a stream terrace is a level strip of an abandoned one. This is {{ref:soil-form-045}} made concrete.

soil-form-157.title: Effective precipitation: why wetter and cooler leaches more
soil-form-157.text: Rainfall alone does not decide how leached a soil is. Precipitation and temperature together set how much water moves down through it. Leaching, described in {{ref:soil-form-050}}, moves soluble salts down the profile and can carry suspended clay into the subsoil, deeper with more precipitation. It lowers pH, removes basic cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+) and lowers nutrient content, so desert soils are little leached and humid forest soils extensively. Higher temperature raises evapotranspiration, so with equal rainfall the cooler region has more effective precipitation and more leached soils. In the Northern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes get less direct sun and so tend to be more weathered, deeper and more leached than warmer, drier south-facing ones. All of this is {{ref:soil-form-044}} in action.

soil-form-160.title: How people change soil
soil-form-160.text: Plow up a forest or grassland and the soil usually loses organic matter; globally about 30% of the original soil organic carbon is lost. Human use transforms soils mainly through land conversion, erosion, mining and construction. Erosion removes the organically enriched surface layer, losing the most fertile soil and sometimes exposing a growth-limiting layer such as a high-sodium one. Where the eroded soil lands, it over-thickens lower slopes and buries the original topsoil under less fertile subsoil, giving a cumulic soil. Soils heavily disrupted by people, as by mining or pipelines, are termed anthropogenic, and reconstructed soils inevitably differ from the original profile. People thus join the {{ref:soil-form-043}}.

soil-form-162.title: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon
soil-form-162.text: No other part of Canada has soils as varied as British Columbia and Yukon, thanks to a varied geologic history, rugged terrain and a wide climate range. The region holds all ten soil orders of the Canadian system. Podzols have the largest extent in British Columbia, on acidic parent materials under cool, humid conditions, and Luvisols are the other dominant order, on loamy glacial tills in the Interior plateaus and boreal forest. Cryosols occur in permafrost areas of northern Yukon and on high mountain peaks, while Chernozems occur only in the arid Central Interior. Regosols mark landslide-prone and avalanche-prone slopes and the Fraser Delta, and drained Gleysols in the Fraser Valley are among the province's most productive farm soils. Mining leaves Anthroposols; in metal mining the chief concern is acid rock drainage, because sulphide minerals such as pyrite weather rapidly to sulfuric acid.

soil-form-166.title: Soils of Ontario
soil-form-166.text: Ontario's soils are young, laid down by the Wisconsinan Laurentide Ice Sheet. The ice retreated northeast, exposing southern Ontario as much as 13,000 years ago and the far north about 8,500 to 6,500 years ago. Three ecozones now dominate. The Hudson Plains (about 25% of Ontario) are cold and semi-arid, with clayey and silty glacio-marine materials over neutral to alkaline limestones. The Boreal Shield (about 66%) lies on acidic, weathering-resistant Precambrian gneiss and granite, and Dystric Brunisols dominate the west. The Mixedwood Plains (about 9%) rest on carbonate-rich limestones, so parent material matters most; they hold the province's most productive farmland and its major cities. The Guelph series, a Brunisolic Gray-Brown Luvisol formed in loam to silt loam moraine, became Ontario's provincial soil in 2015.

soil-form-167.title: Soils of Quebec
soil-form-167.text: Quebec's soils sit in bands from south to north, and there are seven soil orders in them. They formed over the last 6,000 to 10,000 years, after the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated, on parent materials that follow the Canadian Shield, the Appalachians and the sedimentary St. Lawrence valley. Podzols cover 39% of Quebec, Brunisols 17% and Organic soils 8%. Dystric Brunisols can turn into Podzols over several thousand years, as on the North Shore. After glaciation the Champlain Sea left salt-rich clay in the St. Lawrence Lowlands; leaching of the salt and river incision made it unstable, causing over 700 landslides and earthflows. Only a small area has high agricultural potential: Canada Land Inventory Classes 1 to 3 total about 0.28 ha per Quebecer, the smallest of any province, and about 80% of them are cropland, so conserving them matters.

soil-form-169.title: Soils of the Atlantic Provinces
soil-form-169.text: Seven of Canada's ten soil orders occur in Atlantic Canada, but heavy precipitation and coarse, acidic glacial till make Podzols dominant. The soils are often stony or shallow to bedrock, so the four provinces hold only about 1.5% of Canada's farmland, and only Prince Edward Island has more farmland than forest. Four ecozones divide the region. The Atlantic Maritime is warmest, about 7 degrees C with 1250 mm of rain a year, on mostly sedimentary Paleozoic rock. The Taiga Shield and Arctic Cordillera are colder, on Precambrian gneiss and granite with thin till and exposed rock. The Canada Land Inventory finds no Class 1 land here; Class 2 is about 588,000 ha, Class 3 about 2,275,000 ha and Class 4 about 2,507,000 ha, and most of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland is Class 7.

soil-form-163.title: Soils of the Prairie Provinces
soil-form-163.text: In southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, over 80% of the land is agricultural, the most heavily converted in Canada, and the kind of farming follows soil capability. True prairie covers only the southern part. About one-third of the region sits on Canadian Shield rock and two-thirds on sedimentary rock; igneous rock yields acidic sandy, gravelly parent materials, sedimentary rock neutral to alkaline loamy ones. Chernozems dominate the southern grassland, Luvisols the northern mixed forest, Brunisols the acidic Shield and Organic Cryosols the cold, saturated peats near Hudson Bay. The pattern is set by bedrock and by the rain shadow of the Western Cordillera. Crops once centred on spring wheat with summerfallow; today canola, pulses and flax are grown, with continuous cultivation and conservation tillage or no-till. Under the Canada Land Inventory, classes 1 to 4 sustain field crops and classes 5 and 6 suit only forage.

soil-form-165.title: From grassland to forest: the Parkland transition
soil-form-165.text: Walk north from the grassland and the soil changes as tree litter replaces grass as the main organic input. In the transitional Parkland the Ah horizon lightens and begins to bleach, forming an Ahe horizon; these are Dark Gray Chernozems. Further north, in continuous Mixedwood forest, an LFH litter layer sits on the mineral soil over a bleached Ae horizon and a clay-richer Bt horizon, underlain by a carbonate-bearing C horizon. These are Gray Luvisols, which also form on glacio-lacustrine deposits in north-central Manitoba.

soil-form-164.title: Prairie Chernozems and the grasses that made them
soil-form-164.text: Across the Prairies, Chernozemic great groups follow the native grasses, which follow the regional water deficit. They are separated by the color of the A horizon, which shows how much organic carbon the grasses added. In the driest part, with an annual water deficit near 200 mm, low grasses with little biomass give Brown Chernozems; less deficit to the west and north gives Dark Brown and Black ones. Organic carbon is highest in southern Manitoba, where the deficit is only about 70 mm. All have organically enriched Ah horizons over decalcified, slightly reddened Bm horizons.
